We've had other ad hoc projects that have been used in recent years to fill gaps.

Our community organizations in Saskatoon also carry a very heavy load of filling gaps and trying to run programs to address growing needs, but they are also very strained.
We need permanent solutions.
This has been something we've heard from various conversations.

The use of the public washroom trailer that started last year and continued this summer,

We know there's limited access to indoor spaces for cooling and warming and in times of need for air quality protection.

We experience as everyone will know periods of extreme cold in the winter and extreme heat in the summer, and we've also had increasing and extended periods of very poor air quality due to forest fires.
Throughout the summer of 2024 and into 2025, our four main shelters were continuously at capacity.

And some people are just not ready for that step from day one to be able to access those shelters, so they may not access them.
We also have fragmented navigation and support.

There remains inadequate access to ID services, income assistance workers in accessible community locations, community banking access, mail access.

So a community navigation hub network, which is the proposed option in the feasibility study, could be comprised of four main components. Each component could be considered independently as an option or developed together as part of a scaled and phased approach.

A central navigation hub built and operated specifically to provide a full range of supports within the continuum of care. This could be a facility open 247 and would connect individuals with services as needed.
Many hubs and we have two options there. One could be connected with city of Saskatoon Municipal facilities. This could be fire halls, other civic facilities, leisure centers, libraries.
In crease access to basic needs support such as food, washrooms, showers, drinking water, and would have additional support from peacekeepers or outreach workers at the site.
A many hub could be attached to an existing community service provider to increase access to these basic needs supports.

Well, individuals are also accessing the core services of that organization. For example, a many hub could be built into a facility such as the food bank where they would also be able to access the services of that organization, but then get the additional support of the many hub.

The seasonal outdoor hub for individuals such as the public washroom trailer project would allow individuals that are not comfortable or ready to go into a physical space, a navigation center in a more formal way.
But they still need those basic services and to build those relationships with service providers as a first step of entering into the continuum of care.
So this is the type of hub that we've seen operated at comfy with the soviet owner now reach services. Next slide, please.
So in general, the concept of an navigation hub is that individuals in need of a diverse range of services would come to one location to access those services.
So they can come for basic needs, things like washroom access, water access, but also then the services such as housing referrals, ID, mail, income assistance, and various referrals.
So the hub would provide a single location for these types of uses and would allow for indigenous led programming and partnerships to provide culturally relevant support and engagement.
It would provide access to health and housing including connecting clients to health services and into the coordinated access system for referral to stable housing and supports.

The concept of the hub would also be an element of reducing the strain on our various systems. So streamlining some service delivery and reducing the strain on our emergency services, our emergency rooms, police and justice systems, which is currently strangest trying to address some of basic needs, which we could accommodate through a hub system. Next slide, please.

So when we did a scan of these types of facilities, basically across North America, we found a few of the more relevant examples, the which we included in the feasibility study.

Now, particular relevance to us is they're a very close neighbor and very similar conditions. Calgary and Edmonton both have navigation hubs and operation, and we also identified the Harmony House in Houston, Texas.
Calgary and Edmonton have both been developed in the last couple of years. These are efforts led by the province of Alberta, but they have been embedded in facilities.
They are embedded in the Salvation Army facility in downtown Calgary, and then the hub and Edmonton started in an existing building, and has since moved to a larger dedicated facility.

In summary, based on the current context in our community of rising homelessness, this study proposes a navigation hub network model as a new service delivery model in Saskatoon.

The service model of a hub would emphasize a person-centered problem-solving approach aimed to reduce or prevent chronic homelessness by providing coordinated service delivery and individualized support planning.

The model would be intended to fill critical gaps in our current homelessness response system in Saskatoon, and particularly to work to resolve some areas around service fragmentation and access barriers that exist.
